title: The genitive absolute

objectives.can: Recognise a genitive absolute and read it as a clause whose subject is not the subject of the main verb.

explanation.summary: A noun or pronoun in the genitive, joined to a participle in the genitive, makes a small clause of its own: Καταβάντος αὐτοῦ is 'when he had come down'. Its subject is somebody other than the subject of the main verb. It is very common in narrative, where it sets the scene for the next event.

sections.heading: The pattern
body: In the last lesson the participle agreed with the subject of the main verb: ἀκούσας agreed with Ἡρῴδης, and both were nominative. The genitive absolute is the other option. When the participle needs a subject of its own, Greek puts both the subject and the participle in the genitive, and they agree in gender and number. The pair is 'absolute' because it is loosely attached to the sentence: no word of the main clause governs it.

The meaning of the participle is read in the same way as in the last lesson. It may give time, cause, condition, concession or simple circumstance, and the relation is not marked. A present participle often describes something going on at the same time as the main verb, and an aorist participle often describes something that has just happened, but these are tendencies and the passage decides.

sections.heading: Matthew 8:1 as a model
body: Matthew 8:1 begins Καταβάντος δὲ αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ τοῦ ὄρους ἠκολούθησαν αὐτῷ ὄχλοι πολλοί. The participle Καταβάντος is aorist, genitive singular masculine. αὐτοῦ is the pronoun 'he', also genitive singular masculine, and it is the subject of the coming down. The main verb is ἠκολούθησαν, and its subject is a different group, ὄχλοι. So there are two subjects in the sentence, one for each verb, and the genitive marks the one that belongs to the participle.

A useful test is to ask two questions. Who does the participle's action? Who does the main verb's action? If the answers are different, and the first noun and participle are both in the genitive, you are looking at a genitive absolute.

sections.heading: What the subject can be
body: The subject may be a pronoun, as in Matthew 8:1 and John 8:30 (ταῦτα αὐτοῦ λαλοῦντος, 'while he was saying these things'). It may be a full noun, as in Acts 28:3 (τοῦ Παύλου). It may also be a noun that is itself the whole idea, as in Mark 4:35, ὀψίας γενομένης, 'when evening had come'. Here the participle is a form of γίνομαι and the noun ὀψίας is its subject. Expressions of this kind are idioms for time.

The participle may bring other words with it. In John 8:30 the object ταῦτα stands in the accusative, because it belongs to the participle's verb. In Romans 5:6 the participle ὄντων is a form of εἰμί, and ἀσθενῶν is the predicate. The subject, ἡμῶν, is in the genitive.

sections.heading: Look-alikes that are not absolute
body: Several genitive participles are not absolute. If the participle has the article, it is the attributive or substantival participle of the earlier lesson: in Acts 22:9, τοῦ λαλοῦντός μοι is 'of the one speaking to me', the object of a sound that was heard. If a verb such as ἀκούω takes a genitive for the person or thing heard, the genitive noun and participle are governed by that verb: in Acts 6:11, Ἀκηκόαμεν αὐτοῦ λαλοῦντος means 'we have heard him speaking'.

The surest sign is the test given above: the genitive pair has a subject of its own, which the main verb does not share. A participle in the nominative that agrees with the subject of the main verb is the ordinary adverbial participle of the last lesson. In Acts 23:10, γινομένης belongs to an absolute, and φοβηθείς, which comes next, does not.

sections.heading: Why Greek does this
body: The construction lets a writer change the subject without a new sentence. It is especially common in narrative, where a scene or a time is set, then the next event is told: Matthew 8:1, 8:5 and 8:28 all begin this way. In Acts 4:1 the sentence starts with an absolute that sets the apostles speaking before the priests arrive.

The pattern is not without exceptions. Now and then the genitive pair is used although its subject is also the person the main clause is about. In Matthew 1:18 the genitive pair μνηστευθείσης τῆς μητρὸς αὐτοῦ Μαρίας has Mary for its subject, and the main verb εὑρέθη ('was found') is also about her, since ἔχουσα agrees with her. Some grammarians say that this is looser than classical practice. For reading, the useful fact is that the genitive pair still sets a circumstance.

misunderstandings: Taking every genitive participle for an absolute. Check for the article, and for a verb of hearing that governs the genitive.
Treating the genitive pronoun as 'his' or 'of him' in the English sense. In αὐτοῦ λαλοῦντος it is the subject of the participle: 'he was speaking'.
Looking for the subject of the participle in the main clause. By definition the main verb has another subject, and the participle's subject stands with the participle in the genitive.

Reading the tense as absolute time. An aorist absolute usually describes something finished before the main action and a present one something going on at the same time, but these are tendencies, as with all adverbial participles.

deeper.heading: The absolute case in other languages
body: Latin has an ablative absolute that does the same work, and Sanskrit has a locative absolute. In Greek it is the genitive. It is a common way for an inflected language to attach a clause that has its own subject, and the choice of case differs from language to language. It is enough here to know that in Greek the case is the genitive.

deeper.heading: The dative in a similar position
body: Occasionally a participle in the dative, agreeing with a dative noun that the main verb also governs, looks like an absolute. In Matthew 8:23 the dative participle ἐμβάντι is joined to αὐτῷ, and the main clause then uses the same αὐτῷ again. Some grammarians compare such cases to the genitive absolute, as a looser form of the same idea. The genitive absolute is the form you will meet far more often.

examples.analysis: Καταβάντος is an aorist active participle in the genitive singular masculine, and αὐτοῦ is the genitive pronoun that is its subject: 'when he had come down from the mountain'. The main verb is ἠκολούθησαν, whose subject is ὄχλοι, a different subject. The genitive pair sets the scene; the main verb tells what happened next.

quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

examples.analysis: συστρέψαντος and ἐπιθέντος are two aorist participles in the genitive singular masculine, joined by καί, and they share one subject, the noun τοῦ Παύλου: 'when Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and put it on the fire'. The main verb is καθῆψε, and its subject is ἔχιδνα, 'a viper', not Paul. ἐξελθοῦσα, which stands between, is nominative feminine and belongs to ἔχιδνα. It is not part of the absolute.

examples.analysis: ὄντων is the present participle of εἰμί in the genitive plural. Its subject is ἡμῶν, 'we', and ἀσθενῶν, 'weak', agrees with it in the genitive plural. The clause says 'while we were still weak', or, with a shade of cause, 'since we were weak'. The main verb is ἀπέθανεν, and its subject is Χριστός. Two different subjects, and the genitive marks the participle's.

examples.analysis: λαλοῦντος is a present participle, genitive singular masculine, with τοῦ Πέτρου as its subject: 'while Peter was still speaking these words'. The main verb is ἐπέπεσε and its subject is τὸ πνεῦμα. The present participle fits something going on at the same time. Here the subject noun follows the participle; the order is not fixed.

examples.analysis: τοῦ Παύλου λαλοῦντος looks like a genitive absolute, but it is not. The verb ἤκουσεν is a verb of hearing, and verbs of hearing often take the genitive of the person heard. So Paul is the object of 'heard', and λαλοῦντος tells what he was doing: 'this man heard Paul speaking'. The sentence has one subject throughout, οὗτος.

practice.prompt: In Καταβάντος δὲ αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ τοῦ ὄρους ἠκολούθησαν αὐτῷ ὄχλοι πολλοί, which words make the genitive absolute?

quoted.title: Matthew
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: ἠκολούθησαν … ὄχλοι (words 6 and 8): the main verb and its subject
αὐτῷ … πολλοί (words 7 and 9): the dative and the adjective
ἀπὸ τοῦ ὄρους (words 3–5): the prepositional phrase
Καταβάντος … αὐτοῦ (words 0 and 2): the participle and its subject
practice.explain: Both words are in the genitive and agree in gender and number, and they have a subject that differs from that of the main verb ἠκολούθησαν. The other options name the main clause or a phrase.

practice.prompt: In ταῦτα αὐτοῦ λαλοῦντος πολλοὶ ἐπίστευσαν εἰς αὐτόν, who is doing the speaking, and who the believing?

quoted.title: John
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: The one referred to by αὐτοῦ is both speaking and believing
The many are both speaking and believing
ταῦτα is the speaker and πολλοί are the listeners
The one referred to by αὐτοῦ is speaking; the many (πολλοί) are believing
practice.explain: αὐτοῦ λαλοῦντος is the genitive absolute and its subject is the genitive pronoun. The main verb ἐπίστευσαν has the subject πολλοί, so the two actions belong to different people. ταῦτα is the object of the speaking, in the accusative.

practice.prompt: In Καὶ λέγει αὐτοῖς ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ὀψίας γενομένης, what is the subject of the participle γενομένης (word 8)?

quoted.title: Mark
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: αὐτοῖς (word 2), 'to them'
ὀψίας (word 7), 'evening': 'when evening had come'
ἡμέρᾳ (word 6), 'day', in the dative
The subject of λέγει, who is not named in this clause
practice.explain: ὀψίας and γενομένης are both genitive singular feminine, and together they form a genitive absolute for time. The speaker is the subject of λέγει, which is a separate matter.

practice.prompt: μὴ πειθομένου δὲ αὐτοῦ ἡσυχάσαμεν. Whose action does the participle describe, and whose does the main verb?

quoted.title: Acts
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: The participle is a noun meaning 'the unpersuaded one'
Both are about the same people, 'we'
Participle: we would not be persuaded. Main verb: he kept quiet
Participle: he (αὐτοῦ) would not be persuaded. Main verb: we kept quiet
practice.explain: μή negates the participle. The absolute pair μὴ πειθομένου … αὐτοῦ has its own subject, 'he', who is Paul in the verses before. The main verb ἡσυχάσαμεν is first person plural, so the two verbs have different subjects.

check.prompt: Λαλούντων δὲ αὐτῶν πρὸς τὸν λαὸν ἐπέστησαν αὐτοῖς οἱ ἱερεῖς. How does the present participle Λαλούντων (word 0) most likely relate to the main verb ἐπέστησαν?

quoted.title: Acts
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: It gives a purpose: 'in order to speak'
It gives a concession: 'although they spoke'
It describes something long finished: 'after they had once spoken'
It describes something going on at the same time: 'while they were speaking'
check.explain: A present participle often marks something that is going on while the main action happens. The priests came upon them while they were speaking. Nothing in the sentence suggests a purpose or a concession.

check.prompt: καὶ δείπνου γινομένου, τοῦ διαβόλου ἤδη βεβληκότος εἰς τὴν καρδίαν ἵνα παραδοῖ αὐτὸν Ἰούδας. How many genitive absolutes does this verse contain?

quoted.title: John
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: None: both genitive participles belong to the main verb
Three: each genitive word is an absolute
One: δείπνου γινομένου
Two: δείπνου γινομένου and τοῦ διαβόλου … βεβληκότος
check.explain: There are two pairs, each with its own genitive subject and participle: δείπνου γινομένου (a supper taking place) and τοῦ διαβόλου βεβληκότος (the devil having put it in his heart). Neither shares a subject with a main verb in the verse.

check.prompt: Ἀκηκόαμεν αὐτοῦ λαλοῦντος ῥήματα βλάσφημα. Why is αὐτοῦ λαλοῦντος not a genitive absolute here?

quoted.title: Acts
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: Because a genitive pronoun can never be the subject of a participle
Because λαλοῦντος is in the nominative
Because the participle has an article
Because the verb Ἀκηκόαμεν governs the genitive: 'we have heard him speaking'
check.explain: A verb of hearing often takes the genitive of the person heard, so αὐτοῦ is linked to the main verb, and λαλοῦντος tells what he was doing. There is no article, and the case is genitive. The last option is untrue, since the pronoun is the subject of the participle in a real absolute such as Matthew 8:1.

check.prompt: τὴν δὲ φωνὴν οὐκ ἤκουσαν τοῦ λαλοῦντός μοι. Is τοῦ λαλοῦντός μοι (words 14–16) a genitive absolute?

quoted.title: Acts
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: No: the article makes it a participle meaning 'the one speaking', and it depends on φωνήν, 'the voice of the one speaking to me'
No: because μοι is in the nominative
Yes: any genitive participle is an absolute
Yes: because the main verb is in the aorist
check.explain: The article τοῦ shows that λαλοῦντος is a participle used as a noun, in the genitive because it completes φωνήν ('voice of'). A genitive absolute does not have the article with the participle. μοι is dative.

check.prompt: Γενομένης δὲ ἡμέρας ἦν τάραχος οὐκ ὀλίγος ἐν τοῖς στρατιώταις. What does the genitive absolute Γενομένης … ἡμέρας (words 0 and 2) say?

quoted.title: Acts
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: It gives the time: 'when day had come'
It gives a purpose: 'so that day might come'
It names the people who made the disturbance
It is the main verb of the sentence
check.explain: Γενομένης and ἡμέρας are both genitive singular feminine; day is the subject of the participle. The main verb is ἦν, whose subject is τάραχος. The participle sets the time.

check.prompt: πολλῆς δὲ γινομένης στάσεως φοβηθεὶς ὁ χιλίαρχος … ἐκέλευσεν. Which participle is part of a genitive absolute?

quoted.title: Acts
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: φοβηθείς (word 4), because it comes before the main verb
Neither: both are attributive
Both γινομένης and φοβηθείς
γινομένης (word 2), with στάσεως; φοβηθείς is nominative and agrees with ὁ χιλίαρχος
check.explain: γινομένης and στάσεως are both genitive singular feminine and form the absolute: 'when a great disturbance arose'. φοβηθείς is nominative singular masculine and agrees with the subject of ἐκέλευσεν, so it is an ordinary adverbial participle: 'the commander, being afraid'.

check.prompt: ἐλθούσης δὲ τῆς πίστεως οὐκέτι ὑπὸ παιδαγωγόν ἐσμεν. What is the subject of the participle ἐλθούσης (word 0)?

quoted.title: Galatians
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: οὐκέτι (word 4), 'no longer'
ἐσμεν: the 'we' of the main clause
τῆς πίστεως (words 2–3), 'the faith': 'now that faith has come'
παιδαγωγόν (word 6), 'a guardian'
check.explain: ἐλθούσης, τῆς and πίστεως are all genitive singular feminine. The article belongs to the noun πίστεως, not to the participle. The main verb ἐσμεν has a different subject, 'we'.

check.prompt: Κἀκεῖθεν ἐξελθόντος αὐτοῦ ἤρξαντο οἱ γραμματεῖς καὶ οἱ Φαρισαῖοι δεινῶς ἐνέχειν. Who performs the action of ἐξελθόντος, and who that of ἤρξαντο?

quoted.title: Luke
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: He (αὐτοῦ) went out from there; the scribes and Pharisees began to press
The scribes and Pharisees did both
The scribes and Pharisees went out, and he began to press them
He did both
check.explain: ἐξελθόντος αὐτοῦ is the genitive absolute with αὐτοῦ as the subject of going out. The subject of ἤρξαντο is οἱ γραμματεῖς καὶ οἱ Φαρισαῖοι, who are in the nominative. Case shows which noun goes with which verb.

check.prompt: Which statement about the relation expressed by a genitive absolute is the soundest?

quoted.title: Acts
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: It is always time, because the participle is in the genitive
It is always a command, because the subject changes
It is always cause, because the subject is different
The form does not mark time, cause or the rest; the reader chooses from the passage, and in narrative time or simple circumstance often fits
check.explain: As with other adverbial participles, the relation is inferred. In narrative the genitive absolute very often sets a scene or time, as συστρέψαντος … τοῦ Παύλου does here: 'when Paul had gathered the sticks'. Nothing in the form fixes it.

reading.why: Matthew 8:1 and 8:5 each begin with a genitive absolute (Καταβάντος … αὐτοῦ, Εἰσελθόντος … αὐτοῦ) that sets the scene for the main verb, and the verses between them show nominative participles agreeing with the subject, so you can compare the two.
